parts.passage:
The Seed Hunters

How a global network of scientists is racing against time to preserve the world's plant diversity

ADeep in the remote valleys of Central Asia, in the mountain ranges of South America, and across the dryland savannas of sub-Saharan Africa, a quiet but urgent operation is underway. A scattered network of botanists, ecologists, and field collectors — known informally as seed hunters — are combing the world's most biodiverse habitats in search of plant material that may soon cease to exist. Their mission is simple in principle but enormously complex in practice: to collect, catalogue, and safely store seeds from wild plant species before habitat destruction, climate change, or other pressures eliminate them forever.

BThe Millennium Seed Bank Partnership (MSBP), coordinated by the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew in the United Kingdom, is the largest and most ambitious of several global seed conservation programmes. By the end of its first phase in 2009, it had banked seeds from ten percent of the world's wild plant species — over 24,000 species in total. Its current target is to have twenty-five percent of the world's wild plant species in storage by 2020, with particular emphasis on species considered at risk of extinction. Partner institutions in more than eighty countries contribute to the bank's collections, often focusing on plants native to their own regions that are absent from other collections.

CThe process of seed banking is more painstaking than it might initially appear. Not all seeds are suitable for conventional storage — a category of plants known as 'recalcitrant' species produce seeds that die if dried or frozen, making them extremely difficult to preserve using standard methods. Among these are many tropical fruit trees, whose seeds must be kept at precise humidity and temperature levels, or maintained as living tissue cultures. For the majority of species, however, seeds can be cleaned, dried to a moisture content of around three to seven percent, sealed in airtight containers, and stored at minus twenty degrees Celsius. Under these conditions, most seeds remain viable for decades; some species have been successfully germinated after over two hundred years in storage.

DFieldwork is among the most demanding aspects of the seed hunter's role. Collectors must travel to remote and sometimes politically volatile areas, often during narrow seasonal windows when seeds are mature but have not yet dispersed. They must gather samples from multiple individual plants within a population — typically at least fifty — to ensure that the genetic diversity of the species is adequately represented. Collecting too few plants, or selecting individuals that happen to be genetically similar, risks creating a seed bank that preserves the species in name only, without the genetic breadth necessary for long-term survival or adaptation.

ECritics have raised several concerns about seed banking as a conservation strategy. Some argue that it represents a form of 'frozen biodiversity' — a technical fix that allows policymakers to avoid addressing the root causes of habitat destruction. Others point to the risk of institutional failure: seed banks depend on infrastructure, funding, and stable political conditions, none of which can be guaranteed indefinitely. A fire or prolonged power cut at a facility, as has occurred at some regional banks, can destroy decades of irreplaceable material. The global seed vault located inside a mountain in Svalbard, Norway, was designed partly to address this vulnerability, providing a secure backup for collections held in partner institutions around the world. Even Svalbard, however, experienced a minor breach in 2017 when melting permafrost allowed water to enter its access tunnel, prompting urgent repairs and a redesign of the facility's drainage systems.

FDespite these challenges, seed hunters and their supporters argue that the banks play a vital and irreplaceable role. Seeds stored today may prove essential for restoring degraded ecosystems, breeding new crop varieties resistant to drought or disease, or discovering pharmaceutical compounds yet unknown to science. The value of any individual species cannot be known in advance; a plant that appears unremarkable today may turn out to carry genes critical to the agricultural systems of tomorrow. In this sense, seed banking is less a solution to the biodiversity crisis than a form of insurance against our own ignorance — a way of keeping options open in an uncertain future.
